links.title: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System
links.why: The nine-page paper the chapter calls the whitepaper: the double-spend problem, the proof-of-work chain, and the probability table the Confirmation concept recomputes.

links.title: BIP 21 - URI Scheme
links.why: The grammar behind the payment request a wallet shows as a QR code, with the amount and label parameters the Invoice example parses.

links.title: BIP 39 - Mnemonic code for generating deterministic keys
links.why: Where the twelve- and twenty-four-word recovery codes come from: the entropy-to-word table and the key-stretching step that turns the words into a seed.

links.title: BIP 173 - Base32 address format for native v0-16 witness outputs
links.why: The Bech32 encoding and the checksum algorithm the Bitcoin address example runs, including the test vectors a wallet is expected to reject.

links.title: Bitcoin Core :: Bitcoin Core RPC
links.why: The command reference of the reference implementation: every call a running node answers, which is how the chapter's claims can be checked against a real node.

links.title: Bitcoin Core :: Releases
links.why: The release history and the signed checksums to verify a download before running it as a full node.

links.title: Controlled supply - Bitcoin Wiki
links.why: The halving table era by era and the exact total of 20,999,999.9769 bitcoin that the Supply cap example recomputes.

links.title: Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) v1.0
links.why: The identifier the Semantic bridge section connects to Bitcoin's key-holder control: a name whose controller is proved by a key rather than by a registry.

links.title: Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0
links.why: How a signed claim about a subject is expressed, which is the second half of the bridge between this chapter and the semantic web.

links.title: RFC 8018: PKCS #5: Password-Based Cryptography Specification Version 2.1
links.why: The specification of PBKDF2, the key-stretching function a recovery code is passed through, including the advice on iteration counts the chapter cites.

links.title: RFC 6234: US Secure Hash Algorithms (SHA and SHA-based HMAC and HKDF)
links.why: SHA-256 defined with its test vectors, so the hash the chapter prints can be checked against the standard rather than against another program.

links.title: RFC 4648: The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings
links.why: Why a 32-byte hash is written as 64 hexadecimal characters, and what an encoding does and does not change about the bytes underneath.

links.title: RFC 4949: Internet Security Glossary, Version 2
links.why: Careful definitions of the security words this chapter uses in passing, malware and phishing among them, in the vocabulary the internet standards themselves use.

links.title: The Open Source Definition - Open Source Initiative
links.why: The ten conditions a licence must meet to be called open source, which is the test the chapter's claim about the reference implementation has to pass.

links.title: The Bitcoin Lightning Network: Scalable Off-Chain Instant Payments
links.why: The design the Offchain payment and Payment channel concepts summarise, in the draft its own authors published.

links.title: The Byzantine Generals Problem
links.source: Lamport, Shostak and Pease, ACM TOPLAS
links.why: The 1982 paper that states the agreement problem Bitcoin's consensus answers, with the two-thirds bound the chapter quotes.

links.title: Protocol - Glossary | MDN
links.why: A short, careful definition of the word protocol, the term the chapter leans on when it calls Bitcoin a peer-to-peer protocol.

links.title: Phishing - Wikipedia
links.why: The history and the current shapes of the attack the Threats section names, with the signals that identify a counterfeit page.

links.title: Blockstream explorer API: the identifier of block 0
links.why: A live public endpoint that answers with the genesis block's identifier, so the figure the Block concept quotes can be re-checked against the network rather than against this page.

links.title: About us | W3C
links.why: Who publishes the Recommendations the Semantic bridge section cites, and what the word Recommendation means in that organisation's process.

_note: Every address in this list was requested with curl on the date in 'checked' and answered with HTTP 200; the title recorded is the one the answer itself carried - the page's own title element for the HTML pages, the Title line of the document for the three BIPs, and the title printed on the first page for the three PDF papers, each read from the copy saved in 08-tooling/ch01-sources. No video and no discussion thread is listed: none could be opened and read from the build environment. github.com itself answers 403 to this environment, so the three BIPs are linked at raw.githubusercontent.com, which answers 200.
